- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

So, we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186378955 :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-20)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{aligned}]+20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}19 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 27\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-95026062-b044-5134-829b-f9813c55ce41" :question/id #uuid "95026062-b044-5134-829b-f9813c55ce41" :question/math-academy-id "q-170503" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-10.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-10)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}]+10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}11 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

2\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186378969 :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-007e2f87-bfd3-551c-b1fd-ebba47bfe21b" :activity/id #uuid "007e2f87-bfd3-551c-b1fd-ebba47bfe21b" :activity/title "Constrained Optimization of Quadratic Forms: Determining Where Extrema are Attained" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186048933 :activity/course 17592186046660 :activity/steps ["step-196c1ec1-7222-5bfa-b1e9-032cecfa7659" "step-3bf30ed1-f62d-5db0-95c3-bae2ee7a2121" "step-92250051-c04a-54d1-8629-4491dfcb275a" "step-5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" "step-e31c99b8-71b1-5ecf-a2b4-f70c0a3c9f33"] :activity/first-step "step-196c1ec1-7222-5bfa-b1e9-032cecfa7659" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-196c1ec1-7222-5bfa-b1e9-032cecfa7659" :step/id #uuid "196c1ec1-7222-5bfa-b1e9-032cecfa7659" :step/content 17592186388524 :step/next "step-3bf30ed1-f62d-5db0-95c3-bae2ee7a2121" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-3bf30ed1-f62d-5db0-95c3-bae2ee7a2121" :step/id #uuid "3bf30ed1-f62d-5db0-95c3-bae2ee7a2121" :step/content 17592186378955 :step/next "step-92250051-c04a-54d1-8629-4491dfcb275a" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-92250051-c04a-54d1-8629-4491dfcb275a" :step/id #uuid "92250051-c04a-54d1-8629-4491dfcb275a" :step/content "question-95026062-b044-5134-829b-f9813c55ce41" :step/next "step-5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/content 17592186410195 :step/next "step-e31c99b8-71b1-5ecf-a2b4-f70c0a3c9f33" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-e31c99b8-71b1-5ecf-a2b4-f70c0a3c9f33" :step/id #uuid "e31c99b8-71b1-5ecf-a2b4-f70c0a3c9f33" :step/content 17592186378969 :db/ensure [:step/validate]}]

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198562 :question/id #uuid "48e09a9b-efe0-5a6d-96f4-c82dbcd33806" :question/math-academy-id "q-138095" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1512bf0f-a0b6-5737-8456-15bf7348d13a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414668} {:answer/id #uuid "189d044b-20ef-594f-9050-30d36ea1c805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414669} {:answer/id #uuid "3cba96ef-b9b9-582c-9ce3-fb19b45e7859" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414670} {:answer/id #uuid "b75669b6-5915-5577-8d99-85ede9b169dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414671} {:answer/id #uuid "e53e0f0c-01ad-5114-93c5-0442b0a0663a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414668} :answer-field/id #uuid "72e392f4-71c8-5797-8085-77f0d25ff7b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414673}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $3.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

"First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$

17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

 

when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. 

So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Let's check that this is indeed the vector we were looking for: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{\text{max}}) & ={(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-10(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{10}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50ae6a7-1f29-5274-bd82-d2d8acfef6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7954 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "08dd4ae6-a6ab-54da-a4ca-840835781b76" :step/math-academy-id "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{'}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & … & 0\end{aligned}]$ then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

:question/math-academy-id "q-138128" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

$$

$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$

$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "80ab5b9e-fd44-5cd4-b555-7638c14ed974" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410200}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5991713d-c756-5033-8e5a-4d4d4ed69367" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-170515" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "14546d02-e8ca-5bbd-82f2-37c20dd8c152" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414675}} {:db/id 17592186414675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "310e7c10-e8a2-5719-93d8-e4b398b84456"} {:db/id 17592186414676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389629 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33fcc9d7-da26-566b-892f-8ca0dccbf100" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389631} {:answer/id #uuid "a86affbe-00af-5daa-9d5d-d6b4c732cb8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389632} {:answer/id #uuid "da2b263a-4cb7-517f-88b9-8ca97ec6707e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389633} {:answer/id #uuid "b5f8b750-04ea-55ad-b825-30a6ece0925e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389634} {:answer/id #uuid "0ceac102-859c-568b-8eb7-f0592356b505" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389635}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389631} :answer-field/id #uuid "205f15e5-0108-5b4a-888b-1b37b338482c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8daa1f82-58aa-5738-bbe7-9b509869abcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-170411" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$

"First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

"q-170525" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+12{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0b1d2308-18cf-5d1f-9792-a558d12df58b"} {:db/id 17592186422487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198560 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5991713d-c756-5033-8e5a-4d4d4ed69367" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410175} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd4da5f-a084-569f-9c7d-65ba6f2fa2d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410176} {:answer/id #uuid "7a09264a-e062-5b32-b960-ce1fdd0596f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410180} {:answer/id #uuid "a18e2980-f7b3-5399-bdf5-0e6bab2f2d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410183} {:answer/id #uuid "f781d714-082f-5b5c-9033-4f6f86bf4d82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410188}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410176} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a69a67c-d671-56dc-a201-31f05adf2afb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410193}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13f589cb-239b-530f-99ce-e58d907d8d98" :question/math-academy-id "q-136828" :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$

$$

$$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "6c3129e5-b4ea-5dec-8fac-9e628947093f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422490}} {:db/id 17592186422489 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}]+250[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8691c397-86b9-56c4-bc27-77cec1d7f354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422486}} {:db/id 17592186422490 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284632 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f787485-bbf8-5fcc-8585-8b059c6d1316" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186281970} {:answer/id #uuid "30948e13-e0e4-533a-a6f9-5aaa08610944" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186282120} {:answer/id #uuid "ebb4dd99-b1d6-5677-9be4-afce453696e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186283750} {:answer/id #uuid "f22aaf14-e55f-5ffd-ba05-b66de4ba750f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186283802} {:answer/id #uuid "fb81bdb4-f9c2-5f58-a975-316cb82f7bda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186283890}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283890} :answer-field/id #uuid "e275f989-8b1b-539a-87a4-fba67d62a361" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284333}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0bda4f08-ef7b-5966-96c3-3621b7deb316" :question/math-academy-id "q-170412" :question/problem "The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-4{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+14{x}_{3}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. $$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$

:question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 14\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 14\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-24 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & -19 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d3d621c0-f7fd-55c5-881a-bf98c73f81f7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422489}} {:db/id 17592186422489 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}]+250[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8691c397-86b9-56c4-bc27-77cec1d7f354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422486}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization.
